originalText:
Zoyuu
The punishments Ashrakal bestowed on his flawed servants
were often but not always permanent. Transforming a servant
into a hideous thing was meant to teach the consequences of
failure and when the victims had suffered enough, the Witch-
King might restore them to their former form or not. Ashrakal
never wasted potential and if a servant could not serve one
way, the Witch-King would make sure they served in another.
A common punishment for those who disappointed the
Witch-King was to face transformation into a zoyuu. Magic
fused the victim’s limbs and stretched them until they were
forced to slither across the ground like serpents. While the
degree of transformation varied, most were literally turned
into human-headed snakes, with mouths filled with three
rows of tiny fangs, each hollow and capable of injecting
a creature with a powerful toxin. The zoyuu would coil
around the Witch-King’s palace and blanket the steps
leading up to his blackened throne.
The zoyuu who remained after the Witch-King’s death
found themselves trapped in their wretched forms forever.
The Kalasans butchered many, but enough escaped into the
wilderness where they have bred with each other and other
serpents, passing their hideous form to new generations.
Nests of zoyuu can be found in warm wooded areas as well
as in the Desolation.
Zoyuu hate all living things and strike at anyone they
encounter. They lament their tortured existence and fight
to the death, knowing that the end of their existence will
free their souls to become something else. Only spite keeps
them from ending their existence early.
A zoyuu speaks the Dark Speech and might know High
Archaic as well.
ZOYUU DIFFICULTY 100
Size 1 horrifying monster
Perception 14 (+4); shadowsight
Defense 13; Health 75; Insanity —; Corruption 6
Strength 12 (+2), Agility 13 (+3), Intellect 14 (+4), Will 11 (+1)
Speed 10; climber, swimmer
Skirmish When a zoyuu uses an action to attack, its
movement does not trigger free attacks until after the
end of the round.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Fangs (melee) +3 with 2 boons (2d6 plus Venom)
Venom If the target is a creature, it must get a success on
a Strength challenge roll with 1 bane or take 3d6 damage
from the venom and become poisoned. At the end of
each round, a poisoned creature takes 3d6 damage
from the venom and can make a Strength challenge
roll with 1 bane. On a success, the creature removes the
poisoned affliction from itself. If the creature becomes
incapacitated by taking damage from the venom, the
creature dies and its body dissolves into a sticky, foul-
smelling mess.
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Darting Fangs When a creature moves within 2 yards of
the zoyuu, the zoyuu can use a triggered action to attack
the triggering creature with its fangs.
Undead
The Men of Gog delved deeply into the secrets of
Necromancy, devising all manner of ways in which to
trap the soul in the flesh. Initial efforts saw the creation
of animated corpses and zombies, but as the Men of
Gog advanced their understanding of the magic, they
learned how to create grave thralls, boneguard, as well
as vampires, revenants, and Death Lords. “Ascension” to
an undead state was a reward nearly all the Witch-King’s
subjects hoped to achieve, but since Ashrakal wanted to
liberate souls from the Underworld and Hell, he restricted
ascension to those who could no longer sire or bear
children. Each new generation of Gog meant more souls
freed from the faeries, souls that could eventually be
anchored in the world by means of dark magic.

---
20
After Ashrakal’s demise, Gog survivors who returned to
the Desolation threw themselves into harnessing magical
energies from the Obsidian Tombs and using them to
create an undead horde. The initial wave crashed into the
Northern Reach years ago, but were eventually pushed
back. Even now though, ever-vigilant defenders must still
stand the walls of the Crusader States’ citadels overlooking
the wastes, as the undead still emerge in great number from
the swirling dust and sand, seeking to wreak havoc and
death on the lands below.

name: PLAGUE ZOMBIE

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Plague Zombie
Zombies, created by the Disciple Ruiner, carry within
them the means to create more of their kind. Any living
person they bite that subsequently dies will rise soon after
to embark on their own mindless pursuit of flesh and
brains. Undead slayers guard themselves against infection,
armoring their body to prevent becoming contaminated
through the zombies’ bites, but reports of other zombies,
bloated and venting toxic green gas, crawling with flies have
been coming out of the Crusader States. Plague zombies
not only infect, but they explode when struck to spread
contagion everywhere.
PLAGUE ZOMBIE DIFFICULTY 10
Size 1 horrifying undead
Perception 10 (+0); shadowsight
Defense 8; Health 40; Insanity —; Corruption —
Strength 12 (+2), Agility 8 (–2), Intellect 6 (–4), Will 13 (+3)
Speed 8
Immune damage from disease and poison; asleep,
charmed, dazed, diseased, fatigued, frightened,
poisoned, stunned
Injured Outburst If the plague zombie takes damage while
it is injured, roll a d6. On a 4 or higher, the zombie takes
damage equal to its Health and explodes from a point
in its space out into a 5-yard radius. Each living creature
in the area of the explosion must get a success on a
Strength challenge roll with 1 bane or become diseased.
While diseased in this way, the creature cannot heal
damage. If the diseased creature becomes incapacitated,
it dies and, 1d6 rounds later, rises as a plague zombie,
retaining none of its original statistics or abilities. Each
time a diseased creature completes a rest, it must make
a Strength challenge roll with 2 banes. On a failure,
it takes 3d6 damage. On a success, it removes the
diseased affliction from itself.
Toxic Cloud Foul vapors wafting off the plague zombie’s
body spread out and partially obscure a 2-yard-radius
sphere centered on a point within the zombie’s space.
Wind disperses the vapors, causing the zombie to lose
this trait for 1 round.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Fist (melee) +2 (1d6)
END OF THE ROUND
Miasmic Presence Each living creature inside the plague
zombie’s toxic cloud must get a success on a Strength
challenge roll with 1 bane or take 1d6 damage from
disease.
The Immortals
The Witch-King had little need for personal guards, as
powerful as he was, but he employed a cadre of elite
warriors, each augmented by dark spells of his own design,
known as the Immortals. Peerless fighters in their own
right, they drew strength from the evil magic flowing
through their bodies. This magic staved off hunger, thirst,
an even the need to sleep. As well, they could use their
magic to shrug off lethal injuries and repair themselves
if incapacitated. Only by dismantling and burning their
bodies could one destroy them.
Immortals wore black clothing that showed only their
eyes. Silver bracers, wrought with serpent designs covered
their arms, while they cinched wide sashes around their
waists. As far as anyone knows, they never speak.

originalText:
IMMORTAL DIFFICULTY 250
Size 1 undead
Perception 15 (+5); shadowsight
Defense 14; Health 120; Insanity —; Corruption 3
Strength 14 (+4), Agility 14 (+4), Intellect 11 (+1), Will 15 (+5)
Speed 12
Immune damage from cold, disease, and poison; asleep,
disease, fatigued, poisoned; spells from dark magic
traditions
Battle Ready The immortal takes its turn before the player
characters.
Combat Instincts The immortal can use three triggered
actions each round. For two of those triggered actions, it
can only make a free attack.

---
21
21
Nimble Moves When the immortal moves, it ignores the
effects of moving across difficult terrain and makes
sound only if it chooses to do so.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Sword (melee) +4 with 3 boons (3d6 + 2)
Scimitar (melee) +4 with 3 boons (3d6 + 1)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Whirling Assault The immortal makes one attack with each
weapon it is wielding.
Parry Counterstrike When a creature the immortal can
see would attack the immortal with a weapon other
than a firearm, the immortal can use a triggered action
to impose 1 bane on the creature’s attack roll. If the roll
results in a failure, the immortal can make a melee attack
against one creature it can reach as part of the triggered
action it used.
END OF THE ROUND
Regeneration If the immortal is not incapacitated, it heals
2d6 damage.
Dark Rebirth If the immortal is incapacitated, it is not
dead or destroyed. Instead, it becomes dormant for
2d6 rounds, during which time the magic in its body
repairs its injuries. At the end of this time, it heals all
damage, stands up, and can take the next available
turn. If the immortal is dismembered and the body
parts burned in a fire, the immortal loses this trait and
is destroyed.
The Uncrowned
Great and mighty champions of Gog sometimes earned
undeath as a reward for constant service and devotion
to the Witch-King. Often, these people would become
forsaken (see Tombs of the Desolation), who would go on
to lead the undead armies in the name of their master.
With the Witch-King gone, the Death Lords who have
risen to take his place have replaced the fallen forsaken
with new ones, while the old ones have risen in both
power and esteem, serving as the eyes, mouths, and
hands of their masters. These uncrowned masters cow
even the forsaken, who cringe before them and their
dread majesty.
An uncrowned stands nearly seven feet tall and clothes
itself in black garments, the hood hanging so low it
completely conceals its features. The undead carries a
greatsword that bursts into flames when drawn. Often,
an uncrowned rides a blight wyvern to soar above the
dust storms to monitor developments in battle and shriek
commands down to its forces.
Uncrowned speak Dark Speech and High Archaic.

UNCROWNED DIFFICULTY 500
Size 1 frightening undead
Perception 20 (+10); darksight
Defense 12; Health 150; Insanity —; Corruption 9
Strength 16 (+6), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 15 (+5), Will 16 (+6)
Speed 12
Immune damage from cold, disease, and poison; asleep,
disease, fatigued, poisoned
Blighted Body Any living creature that comes into contact
with the uncrowned takes a cumulative –1d6 penalty to its
Health, which remains until the creature completes a rest.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Flaming Greatsword (melee) +6 with 3 boons (6d6 plus
2d6 from fire)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Double Attack The uncrowned makes two flaming
greatsword attacks. It can substitute Keening, Serpents
of Darkness, or Ocean of Rot for one of these attacks.
Keening The uncrowned screams. Each creature within
long range that can hear the scream must get a success
on a Will challenge roll with 1 bane or gain 1d3 Insanity.
Once the uncrowned uses Keening, it must wait 1 round
before it can use it again.
Serpents of Darkness The uncrowned throws open its robes
to release tendrils of inky darkness at up to three creatures
within short range. Each creature must get a success on
an Agility challenge roll with 3 banes or take 4d6 damage
and become impaired for 1 minute. While impaired in this
way, the creature deals half damage on weapon attacks it
makes. Once the uncrowned uses Serpents of Darkness, it
must wait 1 round before it can use it again.
Ocean of Rot The uncrowned calls upon a well of
necromantic energy to wash over its enemies. A pale, gray
light spreads out from a point in the uncrowned’s space
until it reaches a 100-yard radius. Each living creature
that has 1 damage or more takes 2d6 damage from the
festering of its wounds. Once the uncrowned uses Ocean
of Rot, it must wait 1 minute before it can use it again.
END OF THE ROUND
Aura of Menace Each living creature within medium range of
the uncrowned must make a Will challenge roll with 1 bane.
A creature gains 1d3 Insanity on a failure and becomes
frightened for as long as it can see the uncrowned. On a
success, the creature becomes immune to this uncrowned’s
Aura of Menace until after it competes a rest.

The dreaded blight wyverns roost in the heights of the Fire
Peaks, a range of volcanic mountains rising from the edges
of the Desolation. Aggressive beasts, they range above
the mountain slopes in search of sheep, ogres, giants, and

Men of Gog provided competition after ranging into the
mountains to claim their eggs. Once hatched, the Gog raise
the young, training them to bear the uncrowned as riders.
A blight wyvern resembles their kin found in the cold
south, but have hides the color of charcoal and bifurcated
tails that each end in a stinger. They have a pair of wings in
place of arms and their hindlegs end in sword-long talons.

carries for miles.

originalText:
Nosferatu
The nosferatu descend from the early vampires, but were
nearly wiped out in the Hegemony’s fall. In Balgrendia,
a fair number managed to survive. Many of the original
ones fought alongside the Witch-King in his disastrous
effort to conquer Niflheim, while others descend from that
first generation. More susceptible to sunlight than other
vampires, nosferatu hide in caves, deep forests, and in
ruins. They prey on children, luring them into the darkness
from which they never emerge.
Nosferatu have tall, thin bodies with oversized bald
heads. Huge eyes command their face, while their ears are
pointed and resemble bat wings. Normally, their mouths
appear small, but they can stretch their jaws wide to sink
their fangs into their victim’s flesh. Most live as exiles and
outcasts, wearing shabby rags and clothing.
These vampires speak Dark Speech, the Common
Tongue, and High Archaic.
NOSFERATU DIFFICULTY 250
Size 1 horrifying undead
Perception 14 (+4); darksight
Defense 16; Health 75; Insanity —; Corruption 8
Strength 13 (+3), Agility 14 (+4), Intellect 12 (+2), Will 17 (+7)
Speed 12
Immune damage from cold, disease, poison; asleep,
diseased, fatigued, immobilized, poisoned, slowed
Blood Dependent The nosferatu suffers the effects of water
deprivation (Shadow, page 200) if it fails to drink blood.
Fear of the Gods A nosferatu makes attack rolls with 1
bane against targets wearing or wielding holy symbols.
Celestial Vulnerability The nosferatu takes double damage
from Celestial spells and makes challenge rolls to resist
such spells with 1 bane.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Claws (melee) +4 with 2 boons (2d6 plus the target is
grabbed on attack roll 20+)
Fangs (melee) +4 with 2 boons or 4 boons against a
grabbed target (1d6 plus Blood Drain)
Blood Drain If the target is a creature of flesh and blood,
the nosferatu drains its blood, imposing a –3d6 penalty
to the target’s Health score that lasts until it completes
a rest. While the target has this penalty, the target is
also fatigued. The nosferatu heals damage equal to the
amount of the penalty.
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Sinister Call The nosferatu can use an action, or a triggered
action on its turn, to call out to one creature it can
see within medium range. If the target can hear the
nosferatu, make a Will attack roll against the target’s
Will. On a success, the target gains 1d3 Insanity. Instead
of becoming frightened from gaining this Insanity, the
target instead becomes charmed.
Sink the Fangs When a creature becomes grabbed by the
nosferatu, the nosferatu can use a triggered action to
attack that creature with its fangs.
END OF THE ROUND
Burned by Sunlight If the nosferatu is in an area lit by
sunlight, it takes 3d6 damage.

originalText:
Dreamstealer
The kindly old women who sells flowers by the docks, the
scribe hurrying down the street, loaded with scrolls, even
the bored sentry digging in a nostril for hidden treasure:
any and all of them could be dreamstealers. In full daylight,
they appear as anyone else: living, breathing people. They
go about their business in much of the same way that
others do, adept at hiding in plain sight.
But the signs of their passage become evident to those
who know what to look for. Dreamstealers feed on the
emotions of their victims, leaving them drained, fatigued,
feeling dead inside—or simply dead. In places where
neglect shows in peeling paint and in rubbish littering
the street, where crying children are ignored, and the
dead pile up, one might surmise a psychic vampire has
come to town.
Dreamstealers hunt during the day and hide themselves
at night for in the shadows and darkness, their true nature
becomes revealed. The ordinary visage sloughs away to
reveal the pinched features, beady black eyes, and purplish
skin of their kind.
The Men of Gog deemed the dreamstealers to be
failures, but could not bring themselves to destroy
them. The dreamstealers fled Ashrakal’s demesne
and insinuated themselves among other people.
Dreamstealers can breed with humans, and their offspring
is always another dreamstealer. Their mates rarely survive
for long; once the ennui experienced from extended
proximity to these vampires becomes unbearable, they
usually take their own lives.
Dreamstealers speak the Common Tongue.
DREAMSTEALER DIFFICULTY 25
Size 1 undead
Perception 15 (+5)
Defense 11; Health 44; Insanity —; Corruption 7
Strength 11 (+1), Agility 11 (+1), Intellect 13 (+3), Will 16 (+6)
Speed 10
Immune damage from disease and poison; diseased,
fatigued, immobilized, poisoned, slowed
Pass for Human In illuminated areas, the dreamstealer
appears human. If the dreamstealer enters a space
obscured by shadows or darkness, it gains the horrifying
trait for as long as it remains there.
Emotion Dependent The dreamstealer suffers the effects
of food deprivation (Shadow, page 200) if it fails to use
Energy Drain at least once per day.

---
23
23
ATTACK OPTIONS
Sword (melee) +1 with 1 boon (1d6 + 2)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Energy Drain The dreamstealer can use an action to drain
energy from one living creature it can see within medium
range. Make a Will attack roll with 1 boon against the
target’s Will. On a success, the target gains 1 Insanity and
becomes fatigued until it completes a rest. While fatigued,
the target is slowed. If the target is already fatigued, it
gains 1d3 Insanity. A target does not become frightened
from gaining Insanity in this way. Instead, the target
makes attack rolls and challenge rolls with a number of
banes equal to its Insanity total. For each point of Insanity
bestowed, the dreamstealer gains a +5 bonus to Health.
END OF THE ROUND

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Mindkiller
When the necromancers brought the first mindkillers before
the Witch-King, it’s said he recoiled in disgust and ordered
them destroyed. Rather than extend their lives, they had
been transformed into abominations, with only the barest
traces of their humanity intact. The magic had warped them
into monstrous things and filled them with an insatiable
hunger for brains. That some survived testifies to their
resilience and the inability of their makers to control them.
Mindkillers have begun appearing in greater and
greater numbers in the Desolation, leading some to
speculate the Death Lords have rediscovered the means of
creating them, or worse, they have learned to create more
of their own. Using people abducted from the border
lands, the necromantic energy of the creation process
unravels their minds and imbues them with a thirst for
brains and cranial fluid.
Mindkillers come equipped with the tools they need to
get to their prized meal. Their mouths resemble those of
lampreys, being ringed with teeth, but framed by a pair
of strong mandibles that can punch through the bone of
a skull, cracking it to release the precious fluids and brain
meat into their gullets.
The violation of their faces extends to their bodies.
They retain their humanoid shapes, but their flesh is
pale, waxy, and threaded with black streaks. All their
body hair is missing and their genitals appear withered
and freakish. They cannot tolerate sunlight and only
hunt at night, but they also have no concept of restraint,
and many have been destroyed pursuing victims into the
daylight hours.
Mindkillers are effectively immortal, but at the price
of their sanity and identity. Their existence torments
the souls trapped inside their flesh and it grows ever
darker as they commit atrocities to feed their base

resilience and the inability of their makers to control them.

speculate the Death Lords have rediscovered the means of

brains and cranial fluid.

get to their prized meal. Their mouths resemble those of
lampreys, being ringed with teeth, but framed by a pair
of strong mandibles that can punch through the bone of
a skull, cracking it to release the precious fluids and brain
meat into their gullets.

pale, waxy, and threaded with black streaks. All their
body hair is missing and their genitals appear withered
and freakish. They cannot tolerate sunlight and only
hunt at night, but they also have no concept of restraint,
and many have been destroyed pursuing victims into the
daylight hours.

of their sanity and identity. Their existence torments
the souls trapped inside their flesh and it grows ever
darker as they commit atrocities to feed their base
appetites. Mindkillers do not speak, though they seem to
understand the Dark Speech.

originalText:
Balbator
Unlike the other tribes of humans, the Men of Gog had no
experience in building siege weaponry such as catapults or
scorpions. Their attack plan was always to overwhelm the
defenders with sheer numbers of undead first, followed by
living soldiers. When confronted by high walls and boiling
oil, they resorted to using demons. The balbators would
be dragged from their cages and sent forward to crash into
and through the defenders’ walls, knocking them down and
slaughtering everyone they found inside.
Balbators stand up to twenty feet tall and weigh many
thousands of pounds. They have hunched postures and
features that resemble wolves, raptors, and bears, but with
a confusion of twisting horns reaching out from the back
of their skulls. Two long bone blades sprout nine feet out
from the backs of their forearms, which they use with dread
efficiency to cut through their enemies. Worst, though, is
the mass of writhing tentacles that erupt from where their
genitals ought to be. These snapping appendages can grab
grown men and pull them into the horrific shadow within
the demon, a maw that leads straight into the Void itself.
BALBATOR DIFFICULTY 750
Size 4 horrifying demon
Perception 12 (+2); truesight
Defense 17; Health 150; Insanity —; Corruption —
Strength 18 (+8), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 11 (+1), Will 18
(+8)
Speed 16
Immune damage from disease or poison; dazed, diseased,
fatigued, frightened, immobilized, impaired, poisoned,
slowed, stunned
Spell Defense A demon takes half damage from spells.
When a creature attacks a demon with a spell, the
demon imposes 1 bane on the attack roll and the demon
makes the challenge roll to resist the spell with 1 boon.
Demonic Shadows Lit areas out to Size + 1 yards around
the demon become shadows. Illumination from spells of
rank 2 or higher suppress these shadows.

Arm Blade (melee) +8 with 3 boons (6d6 or 36 damage to
objects)
Shadow Tentacles (melee) +8 with 3 boons (4d6
damage, and the target becomes impaired for 1 minute;
if the damage would cause the target to become
incapacitated, the balbator drags the target’s body into
the Void where it is devoured by demons).
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Triple Strike The balbator make three attacks: two with its
arm blades and one with its shadow tentacles.
Crashing Stomp The balbator uses an action, or a triggered

originalText:
Hujeta
After several uprisings against the Hegemony, the Witch-
King commanded his demonologists to create tireless
spies to search out disloyal subjects and destroy them.
Months later, the demonologists returned with the hujeta,
a breed of demon that could stay aloft indefinitely and
came equipped with keen eyesight capable of discerning
the smallest details. Although difficult to create, scores of
them constantly patrolled the skies over much of Ashrakal’s
kingdom, neutralizing many threats before they could
bring harm to the new order.
Hujeta resemble large ravens, but with a single giant,
swiveling eyeball in place of a head, and wingspans of
sixteen feet. The demons could shine a fell light from their
eyes and anything illuminated became rooted to the spot,
allowing allies on the ground to find and capture whoever
was being pursued.
HUJETA DIFFICULTY 250
Size 2 horrifying demon
Perception 20 (+10); truesight
Defense 19; Health 60; Insanity —; Corruption —
Strength 11 (+1), Agility 15 (+5), Intellect 10 (+0), Will 12 (+2)
Speed 18; flier (swoop)
Immune damage from disease or poison; dazed, diseased,
fatigued, frightened, immobilized, impaired, poisoned,
slowed, stunned
Spell Defense A demon takes half damage from spells.
When a creature attacks a demon with a spell, the
demon imposes 1 bane on the attack roll and the demon
makes the challenge roll to resist the spell with 1 boon.
Demonic Shadows Lit areas out to Size + 1 yards around
the demon become shadows. Illumination from spells of
rank 2 or higher suppress these shadows.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Claws (melee) +5 with 3 boons (4d6)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Fell Gaze The hujeta can use an action, or a triggered
action on its turn, to gaze at one creature or object it can
see within extreme range. A pale light falls on the target
and everything within 3 yards of it until the hujeta looks
away (not an action) or the huteja moves to a position
where it does not have an unobstructed path to the
target. Each creature in the light must get a success on a
Will challenge roll with 3 banes or become immobilized
for as long as it remains in the light.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Void Step The demon uses an action, or a triggered action
on its turn, to teleport to a space it can see within
medium range. Roll a d6. On a 1, the demon must wait 1
minute before it can use Void Step again.
END OF THE ROUND
Instability If the hujeta is injured, roll a d6. On a 4 or higher,
it becomes a medium demon with flier trait and the
same damage total.

immortals in order to free all mortals from the cruel wheel

eternally travel. They reject all gods, believing them to
be naught but jumped-up immortals who have beguiled
mortals through awe or fear into worshiping them. The

Magog believe, is to destroy all false gods, tear down their
temples, and purge religion in all its forms from the world.

neighboring nations avoid voicing their hostility to
religions, and as needed, will go through the motions of
belonging to a faith to avoid arousing suspicion. No Men of
Gog, though, would ever become willing supplicants of a
deity and thus are never priests.

inevitability of their death and what awaits them in the
afterlife. Their legacy of spitting in Father’s Death’s eye

rather than the oblivion of the Underworld. For this reason,
the descendants are open to anything that would extend
their lifespans or secure their souls against the horror
waiting for them.

specifically the dark arts, to anchor their souls on Urth or
to extend their lifespans. In the Patchwork Lands and the
Kingdom of Skulls, these dabblers strive to transition from
life to death as quickly as possible to free themselves from
the anxiety they feel about dying. In more civilized areas,
such practices are not tolerated and so they must conduct
their studies in secret.

religions forces Gog’s children to hide their natures and
keep their efforts concealed. Resentment over having to
live in secret fosters hatred in some, madness in others,
and these broken people tend to be the most likely to join

annihilation of all things. The Brotherhood of Shadows, the

people of direct descent from the original Magog.

fits. Religion has always been part of the fabric of human

knees to the false gods of other humans and they remained
steadfastly opposed to any kind of devotion with one
exception.
Men of Gog idolize their heroes, whether they are
their venerated ancestors, fearless warriors, or powerful
magicians. Rather than offer up prayers or develop an
orthodoxy around these figures as do the dwarfs, the Men
of Gog recount the exploits and achievements of their
ancestors and take inspiration from them. They tell these
stories of those who came before them to fill themselves
with the courage to become something more than

names spoken alongside those of the Witch-King, Laughter,
Poison, the Dark Lady, and countless others.

Sorrows marks the most defining moment of the Empire,
with Eronymous’s defeat of Ashrakal in single combat—
styled ever after as the great liberator slaying the worst
villain to have ever walked the world—having served to
legitimize nearly nine centuries of Kalasan rule. For the
Men of Gog, however, the death of their champion remains
a point of deep and abiding shame, one that fills them with
hopelessness and dread, since in those days they believed
Ashrakal to be Amaral reborn.

different stories about what happened and have come to
believe in them as if they were the truth. And, who can
say what really happened nearly a thousand years ago?

a distant land to find the magic he needed to destroy the
invaders. Some have even said Ashrakal was not in fact

Lord finds its roots in the old aristocracy of the

darkness than did their fellows, searching the
darkness of the Void for meaning and power.

give them dominion over Urth until such time
that it came forth to devour all of creation. The
Brotherhood of Shadows remains active in and
around the Empire, hatching terrible plots that
drag the world deeper into the shadow of the
Demon Lord. For more information on this cult,
see The Hunger in the Void.

Rûl, from the Desolation to the Dark Lady’s realm, and
everywhere in between. Most heirs are generally humans,

characters found in the Shadow of the Demon Lord rulebook.

blood of Gog in their veins. For more characters of Gog
heritage, be sure to check out Kingdom of Skulls.

originalText:
Blighter
After the fall of the Witch-King and the flight of many
Men of Gog back to the Desolation, despair gripped many
survivors. Among them were those whose disappointment
stabbed so deep that their minds snapped, seeing little
point in trying to save the world from the immortals as
their creator Magog desired. Instead, they came to believe
it was better to simply destroy it all, reducing it completely
to ash and dust. The blighters formed out of this group,
developing techniques to draw magic from the land itself to
power their dread spells of destruction.
With the Men of Gog in the old kingdom having either
become undead or slaves to the Death Lords, few remain to
stop the blighters and their insane designs. The blighters
have quietly climbed the ranks, demonstrating their merit
to their undead lords, and now lead many of the undead
armies mustering in the wastes for the coming invasion.
When freed from the shifting sands, blowing dust, and the
overweening will of the Death Lords, the blighters will then
set in motion their plans to destroy the lands of the living
and all who dwell there.
Blighters wear dusty, tattered, sun-bleached cloaks
overtop rags. They neglect their bodies, which shows in the
sores around their mouths, the fissures in their skin, and
the scabs that dot their bodies. They move about with a
shuffling gait, making it difficult to pick them out within a
crowd of undead thralls.

originalText:
Demon-Binder
The Men of Gog summoned and bound demons to great
effect, arguably practicing the art at a level far beyond
what any other peoples on Urth may have accomplished.
Having discovered and perfected the arts of Demonology
from the troll ruins, the Gog demon-binders showed little
restraint when it came to calling forth nightmares from
the Void, releasing them to devastating effect against
their enemies. The practice of binding demons fell off
considerably after the fall of the Witch-King, but their art
remains alive and well in the few enclaves that remain in
the wastes of the Desolation.
The demon-binders of Gog kept alive the ancient lore,
passing down their lore to apt pupils of great promise and
firm resolve. No matter how balanced their minds might
have been at the beginning of their apprenticeship, the
study of one of the blackest forms of magic takes its toll.
Nearly all demon-binders wear their madness openly,
their bodies bearing horrid script of the names of things
they have released from the Void, and the terrible doom
awaiting them if their souls are lucky enough to wend
their way to Hell, instead of being sucked into the eternal,
indescribable suffering of the Void.

The Witch-King’s Disciples enforced his will in the
Hegemony and ruled over the territories given to them,
some wisely but most tyrannically. The first Disciples
were those who supported the Witch-King’s rise to power
in Magog, helping him lead his great host south into the
invasion of Rûl. Whenever a Disciple died, the Witch-King
would select another worthy follower to fill the vacancy,
bestowing on them certain powers, along with an alias that
suited their talents to help conceal their true names against

originalText:
Dread Cabalist
The Witch-King’s Disciples were among the most powerful
users of magic in the Hegemony, but, like their master,
each depended on a following of apprentices who formed
the Disciple’s cabal. Most cabalists perished in the fighting
and so those who claim the mantle do so without the
anointment of the Disciples who once led them. Instead,
they scour the world for secrets left by their forebears so
they can reach the same heights of magical power of their
predecessors.
Dread cabalists dwell in the vastness of the Desolation,
often found in the service of gorgons, lamias, Death Lords,
or the ancient vampire kings and queens who ruled Magog
long ago. Cabalists make themselves indispensable to
their masters, offering wisdom and council as needed and
magical support when not. When the armies of Gog march,
one can usually find a few dread cabalists flying overhead.
DREAD CABALIST DIFFICULTY 250
Size 1 human
Perception 14 (+4); shadowsight
Defense 18; Health 80; Insanity 5; Corruption 6
Strength 13 (+3), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 14 (+4), Will 14 (+4)
Speed 12; flier
Spell Savant When the dread cabalist casts an attack spell,
it makes the attack roll with 2 boons and imposes 2
banes on challenge rolls made to resist the spell.
ATTACK OPTIONS

SPECIAL ATTACKS
Seeking Darkness The dread cabalist can use an action,

challenge roll. On a success, the spell has no effect on

or higher, the cabalist regains the casting of a spell of the

Exquisite One
Many of the Gog believe the mortification of the flesh
brings clarity. Most scourge their bodies with whips and
chains, piercing their flesh and hanging weights from
hooks embedded in their skin. The Exquisite Ones take
this custom to its extreme, brutalizing their bodies such
that they live in constant, excruciating pain, finding it
difficult to sleep or, really, do much of anything. However,
the Exquisite Ones regard their self-inflicted torment as a
key to unlocking their hidden potential, to stir the demonic
spirit within them, carried in their blood since the creation
of the Hundred, in order to use its power.

and show their foul knowledge in the wreckage of their
bodies. All have abused themselves beyond recognition,
but the methods vary. Some use metal prongs to separate
the flesh or clamps to cause it to bulge in blue-black ridges.
Hooks, barbs, chains, bars, and spikes festoon their flesh,
pulling and tearing, spreading and rending them so that

originalText:
Fallen
Because they were created by the great genie Magog with
demonic essence, within every Man of Gog lies the seed
of unwelcome transformation, the potential to lose their
humanity and become something other and lesser than
human. One need only look to the horde of beastmen
terrorizing the lands or the degenerate troglodytes who
boil out of the depths to see what awaits the Gog if such
a transformation takes hold. The transformation from
human into something other rarely happens overnight.
Often, it is a slow, painful process that erodes sanity in time
with the warping of flesh and soul. Those Men of Gog who
become caught in the process of transformation are known
as the Fallen, for it is believed they have lost their way by
succumbing to the shard of the demonic spirit that makes
up a part of their soul.
The Fallen retain their humanoid forms, but with obvious
signs of demonic corruption. Most will face an existence
as a beastman, with hints and signs in their features of
their futures, such as the sprouting of small horns in their
foreheads, or snout-like noses and mouths, faces covered in
patchy, bristly fur. They are usually unstable and aggressive,
tending to lash out at all around them, particularly those
who manifest no signs of bestiality. Most Fallen eventually
leave behind their people, instinctively seeking out beastmen
to live among, rising as leaders among them because of their
relatively superior intellect and abilities.

Perception 11 (+1); shadowsight
Defense 14 (hard leather, large shield); Health 11; Insanity 4;
Corruption 3
Strength 11 (+1), Agility 10 (+0), Intellect 9 (–1), Will 9 (–1)
Speed 10
Erratic Whenever the fallen gets a failure on an attack roll

boon for 1 round.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Spear (melee or short range) +1 with 1 boon (1d6)

originalText:
God-Hunter
Hatred for the immortal peoples still burns hot in the
hearts of the Men of Gog, despite the millenia since
the birth of the Hundred. Because of that portion of
them that is human and mortal, most focus on the
needs of survival. Some, however, have the original
hate of Magog burning within them, and seek nothing
but to continue their struggle against the faeries, trolls,
and other immortals. Called god-hunters, these Men
of Gog spend their lives training to prowl the sylvan
realms in search of immortal victims to kill. They have
devised certain techniques to protect themselves from
faerie witchery, easily shrugging off their charms and
piercing their glamours so that they can close in and
destroy their immortal victims with swift strokes of their
iron weapons, forged in hate and malice to make their
victims’ suffering all the more worse.
God-hunters work singly or in small teams. They cover
themselves in iron armor that grows rusty with all the
blood they have spilt, bearing many trophies from their
kills—strings of dead atomies to the severed heads of elf
lords and ladies. God-hunters have a grim cast to their
faces and an aura of horrid death, visible to any immortal,
surrounds them, striking fear in any unfortunate enough to
encounter them.
GOD-HUNTER DIFFICULTY 100
Size 1 human
Perception 11 (+1)
Defense 17 (plate and mail); Health 60; Insanity 5;
Corruption 7
Strength 14 (+4), Agility 10 (+0), Intellect 11 (+1), Will 13 (+3)
Speed 8
Certainty of Death If a faerie or troll that can see a god-
hunter is within medium range when it takes its turn, the
creature must make a Will challenge roll with 1 bane. The
creature becomes frightened for 1 minute on a failure, or
becomes immune to all god-hunters’ certainty of death
traits until the creature completes a rest.
Immortal Foe A god-hunter makes attack rolls against
faeries and trolls with 3 boons.
Pierce Illusion A god-hunter who sees or hears an illusion
automatically recognizes it for what it is.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Battleaxe (melee) +4 with 2 boons (3d6 + 2)
Javelin (melee or medium range) +4 with 2 boons (3d6)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Double Attack The god hunter uses an action to make two
weapon attacks.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Steely Resolve If the god-hunter would become charmed,
frightened, or cursed, it can use a triggered action to
make a Will challenge roll with 1 boon. If the source of
the affliction is a Fey or Forbidden spell, the god-hunter
makes the roll with 2 additional boons. On a success, the
god-hunter is not charmed, frightened, or cursed.

Reviled
The descent into corruption and madness brought on
by a serious study of Forbidden magic wreaks havoc
upon the student’s mind and body, usually leaving the
seeker of unspeakable knowledge a broken and shattered
individual. The Reviled come from those ranks of
students who receive special preparation before delving

how to secure their minds and safeguard their souls
from the worst of the magic’s blight. But while they can
cast those foul spells safely, they eventually become
more and more removed from the world, as if reality
itself were rejecting them.
The Reviled exist in a phase state, only partly present in
the world, drifting across the ground as they are repelled
by the land’s abhorrence to their foul nature. Most Reviled

Occult Philosophy
Revenants
One of the last and most successful attempts at keeping
souls from passing into the immortal-crafted afterlife came
in the form of the revenant. The first few managed to refuse
Father Death by their force of will alone. Rather than slip
away, their souls clung to the flesh and gave them a new life,
one in which they were both alive and not. The possibility
of a dead person returning as a revenant does not alone
belong to the Men of Gog, as one can find examples of
their kind throughout all of Rûl. When the Men of Gog’s
necromancers discovered this possibility, they began to
instruct whatever living they could in how to prepare their
minds for their eventual demises. Most were not able to
escape Hell’s clutches, but enough have been successful to
make revenants a noticeable number of the Men of Gog’s
surviving population.

originalText:
Revenant Assassin
The Death Lords of Magog frequently dispatch revenant
assassins into the distant lands to eliminate people in
positions of power within the faiths and churches of
human communities who they believe could impede their
ultimate agenda. These assassins are bound to the sole
purpose of slaughtering anyone affiliated with the temples
or organizations of the religion specifically targeted. With
that said, the assassins make no distinction between
religions and consider anyone proselytizing a faith to be
an enemy of the Gog should they stand in the way of their
designated victims.
REVENANT ASSASSIN DIFFICULTY 100
Size 1 revenant
Perception 12 (+2); darksight
Defense 14 (mail); Health 60; Insanity 5; Corruption 3
Strength 13 (+3), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 10 (+0), Will 11 (+1)
Speed 10
Immune damage from disease and poison; diseased,
fatigued, poisoned
Execution When an injured, surprised, or frightened
creature takes damage from the revenant assassin’s
attack, the creature must get a success on a Strength
challenge roll or take 2d6 extra damage.
Surprising Return When the revenant would become
incapacitated, roll a d6. On a 6, the revenant appears
dead for 1 round. After, it heals 2d6 damage and stands
up. The revenant makes attack rolls with 1 boon for
1 round.
One Foot in the Grave A revenant heals half damage from
magic and potions.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Sword (melee) +3 with 2 boons (2d6 + 2 plus Poison)
Hatchet (melee or short range) +3 with 2 boons (2d6 plus
Poison)
Crossbow (long range) +2 with 2 boons (3d6 plus Poison)
Poison If the target is a creature, it must get a success
on a Strength challenge roll with 2 banes or become
poisoned. If the target is already poisoned, it takes 3d6
damage from the poison instead. While poisoned in
this way, the target is impaired and takes 1d6 damage
at the end of each round. At the end of each round, a
poisoned target can repeat the Strength challenge roll
and removes the effect from itself on a success.
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Double Attack The revenant either attacks with its
crossbow and reloads or makes two attacks: one with its
sword and the other with its hatchet.
Eyes of the Underworld A revenant can use an action to
lock eyes with one creature within short range that it can
see and that can see it. Make a Will attack roll against
the target’s Will. On a success, the target becomes
frightened for 1 minute. On a failure, the target becomes
immune to this revenant’s Eyes of the Underworld until
the target completes a rest.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Quick Reflexes On the revenant’s turn, it can use a
triggered action to hide or retreat.

Few Death Lords will take leave of the protection of their
Obsidian Vaults to take charge of their armies directly.
Instead, they rely on the cabalists and other gifted servants
to shepherd the mindless undead off to battle. Helping in
this effort are a number of revenants who have become
obsessed with their own quasi-undead states, continuing
to delve into the secrets of Necromancy. These foul
individuals revel in darkness and are bound to have many
despicable interests beyond simply animating corpses.

Size 1 frightening revenant
Perception 14 (+4); darksight

Strength 12 (+2), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 14 (+4), Will 11 (+1)

for 1 round. After, it heals 2d6 damage and stands up. The
revenant makes attack rolls with 1 boon for 1 round.

lock eyes with one creature within short range that it can

Occult Philosophy
Mongrels and
Degenerates
The Men of Gog contended with physiological and
anatomical changes not long after they first entered the
Desolation. The imbued hatred from their creator Magog
for the immortals poisoned their hearts and the nascent
magic they first encountered, polluted by the Hateful
Wars between the trolls and faeries, fed upon their inner
darkness. Many showed physical signs of their corruption
in the telltale marks of darkness that afflict any who
embrace evil—but even these would only be warning signs
of the beginning of the transformations that will harass
them until the end of time itself.
Beastmen
Sources conflict about the true origins of the beastmen.
Some claim they descended from the Men of Gog,
degenerated by the foul magic they used. Others suggest
that they, along with other First Peoples, were turned into
beastmen by the faeries. A few heretics claim the beastmen
were the first aborted efforts of the genies to create humans.
All or none of these stories could be true, but, without a
doubt, certain kinds of beastmen are directly connected
to the Men of Gog. Specifically, the anubin (see Tombs
of the Desolation), those jackal-headed marauders of the
Desolation, were exiled from Gog to control what was
believed to be a malady that had broken out among their
ranks upon their exodus into the Desolation.
After being driven out, the anubin formed into large
tribes and began to prowl the edges of the Desolation’s
wastes, sometimes pressing south to harass the settlers
or to hunt fresh game, human or otherwise. The anubin
have frequently clashed with the Men of Gog, though they
have never managed to gather in numbers sufficient to be
considered a significant threat to the kingdom of Magog.
Instead, the anubin raided their settlements for slaves, food,
and supplies before melting back into the sands once more.
Although beastmen continue to live in the borderlands
north and west of the Witch-King’s former capital of
Maelfax, now called Caecras by the Kalasans, the Gog
exiles fleeing the victors’ pursuit sought whatever refuge
they could find in these untamed lands. It’s believed that
the Gog refugees swiftly surrendered to their demonic
impulses and mingled with the beastmen, breeding
offspring of more variety and horror than previously seen
in the world. Gog relics uncovered by imperial forces who
finally tamed some of these lands to found Tear suggest
some truth to these grotesque tales.
Mogs
The corruption-born trait responsible for the
transformation of many Men of Gog into beastmen also
afflicted the refugees who fled the founding of the Empire.
Fearful of returning to the Desolation, some vanished into
the hot wetlands of the Northern Reach, where they built
crude societies deep in the swamplands to escape and hide
from the retribution they feared. Generations of inbreeding
and debased behavior saw the Gog here shed their
humanity and submit to the beast within. Called mogs,
their original heritage has all but been obscured by their
resemblance to frogs. They stand twice as tall as humans,
having become bloated by their inner darkness, with moist
skin, wide mouths, and great bulging eyes.
In addition to their lost humanity, mogs have severed
all ties to civilization. They have become so reduced and
backwards that they live almost like animals. Most mog
communities, the few that exist, form around old altars
or monoliths found within the swamps, or those relics
that were dragged there. These stones have become their
gods and when night falls, they gather round them and
sing a horrid croaking song to invoke favor from whatever
monstrous deity they believe still lurks within. Some mog
communities still fashion crude shelters, but as they have
slid further and further into savagery, many simply do
without.
Mogs speak a crude, limited version of the Dark Speech,
a croaking, guttural tongue that gives them a bare means of
communicating with one another.

the target completes a rest.

Restore the Dead The revenant necromancer takes 1d6
damage and each undead friendly to it and within short
range of it heals the same amount of damage as taken
by the necromancer.

an action, or a triggered action on its turn, to let one
friendly undead within short range use a triggered action
to perform any activity that would normally require the
use of an action.

Power 3
Necromancy mark of the necromancer (4) O
, spectral grasp
(4), animate corpse (2), bone armor (1) O
, bone splinters
(1), shrieking skull (1), keening (1) O
O
Occult Philosophy
Mongrels and
Degenerates
The Men of Gog contended with physiological and
anatomical changes not long after they first entered the
Desolation. The imbued hatred from their creator Magog
for the immortals poisoned their hearts and the nascent
magic they first encountered, polluted by the Hateful
Wars between the trolls and faeries, fed upon their inner
darkness. Many showed physical signs of their corruption
in the telltale marks of darkness that afflict any who
embrace evil—but even these would only be warning signs
of the beginning of the transformations that will harass
them until the end of time itself.
Beastmen
Sources conflict about the true origins of the beastmen.
Some claim they descended from the Men of Gog,
degenerated by the foul magic they used. Others suggest
that they, along with other First Peoples, were turned into
beastmen by the faeries. A few heretics claim the beastmen
were the first aborted efforts of the genies to create humans.
All or none of these stories could be true, but, without a
doubt, certain kinds of beastmen are directly connected
to the Men of Gog. Specifically, the anubin (see Tombs
of the Desolation), those jackal-headed marauders of the
Desolation, were exiled from Gog to control what was
believed to be a malady that had broken out among their
ranks upon their exodus into the Desolation.
After being driven out, the anubin formed into large
tribes and began to prowl the edges of the Desolation’s
wastes, sometimes pressing south to harass the settlers
or to hunt fresh game, human or otherwise. The anubin
have frequently clashed with the Men of Gog, though they
have never managed to gather in numbers sufficient to be
considered a significant threat to the kingdom of Magog.
Instead, the anubin raided their settlements for slaves, food,
and supplies before melting back into the sands once more.
Although beastmen continue to live in the borderlands
north and west of the Witch-King’s former capital of
Maelfax, now called Caecras by the Kalasans, the Gog
exiles fleeing the victors’ pursuit sought whatever refuge
they could find in these untamed lands. It’s believed that
the Gog refugees swiftly surrendered to their demonic
impulses and mingled with the beastmen, breeding
offspring of more variety and horror than previously seen
in the world. Gog relics uncovered by imperial forces who
finally tamed some of these lands to found Tear suggest
some truth to these grotesque tales.
Mogs
The corruption-born trait responsible for the
transformation of many Men of Gog into beastmen also
afflicted the refugees who fled the founding of the Empire.
Fearful of returning to the Desolation, some vanished into
the hot wetlands of the Northern Reach, where they built
crude societies deep in the swamplands to escape and hide
from the retribution they feared. Generations of inbreeding
and debased behavior saw the Gog here shed their
humanity and submit to the beast within. Called mogs,
their original heritage has all but been obscured by their
resemblance to frogs. They stand twice as tall as humans,
having become bloated by their inner darkness, with moist
skin, wide mouths, and great bulging eyes.
In addition to their lost humanity, mogs have severed
all ties to civilization. They have become so reduced and
backwards that they live almost like animals. Most mog
communities, the few that exist, form around old altars
or monoliths found within the swamps, or those relics
that were dragged there. These stones have become their
gods and when night falls, they gather round them and
sing a horrid croaking song to invoke favor from whatever
monstrous deity they believe still lurks within. Some mog
communities still fashion crude shelters, but as they have
slid further and further into savagery, many simply do
without.
Mogs speak a crude, limited version of the Dark Speech,
a croaking, guttural tongue that gives them a bare means of
communicating with one another.

originalText:
Great Mog
Every generation, mogs spawn a throwback to an earlier
incarnation of their kind, one that has not slid so far into
degeneracy. These so-called “blue mogs” have bright blue
skin and smaller bodies than do their kindred, but they
are far smarter and have innate magical abilities of vital
importance to their tribes. Their hatching is immediately
recognized as a cause for great celebration among the mogs,
who will then sacrifice a great many slaves, offering up
the brains as gifts to their newborn great mog. The bands
always look to these mystics for leadership, doing whatever
they can to exalt and protect them.
GREAT MOG DIFFICULTY 50
Size 1 monster
Perception 15 (+5); shadowsight
Defense 11; Health 45; Insanity 5; Corruption 6
Strength 11 (+1), Agility 11 (+1), Intellect 11 (+1), Will 12 (+2)
Speed 10; swimmer
Immune damage from disease; diseased
ATTACK OPTIONS
Teeth (melee) +1 with 1 boon (1d6 + 2)
Claws (melee) +1 with 1 boon (1d6 + 1)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Double Attack The great mog attacks with its teeth and its
claws. It can cast a spell in place of its claws attack.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Dread Command When a mog ally within medium range
would attack, the great mog can use a triggered action
to grant 2 boons on the creature’s attack roll. If the
attack roll results in a failure, the triggering creature
becomes stunned for 1 round.
MAGIC
Power 5
Forbidden carve the flesh (6) O
, seal the cavity (3) O
,
serpent tongue (3) O
, ravenous maggots (2), vision’s end
(2), unruly organs (2) O
, vivisection (2) O
, spectacular
expulsion (1) O
, hook the soul (1) O
O
Occult Philosophy.
END OF THE ROUND
Startled Leap When a creature within short range of the
mog takes a fast turn, the mog can use a triggered
action to jump 1d6 yards away from the triggering
creature. This movement does not trigger free attacks.
Troglodytes
The darkness of Gog remains alive and well in
underground warrens all across Rûl. In these dark, noisome
places dwell the troglodytes, a race of degenerate people
whose descent is arguably claimed from the Men of Gog
who sought refuge by hiding in the depths of the earth.
Centuries of inbreeding and dark magic have transformed
them into hideous monsters who kill with merciless
abandon. Under the cover of darkness, they creep from
their lairs to murder and steal, dragging people into
their foul realms, subjecting them to unspeakable and
indescribable torments. Troglodytes receive extensive detail
in Wretched and Unclean, a Monstrous Pages supplement.
